blocks.instruction: Complete the summary below. Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.

people.name: Talia Gunawardena
people.role: marine ecologist who led a five-year survey of transplanted corals

people.name: Sione Lautaha
people.role: fisheries researcher who studied a village-run restoration project in the Pacific

people.name: Lars Edvardsen

paragraphs.text: Coral reefs occupy less than one percent of the sea floor, yet they shelter roughly a quarter of all known marine species, protect coastlines from waves and support fisheries and tourism on which hundreds of millions of people depend. Over recent decades, however, many reefs have lost a large share of their living coral, and in some regions the reef that divers see today is a grey, weed-covered skeleton of what existed a generation ago. Against this background, a growing number of projects aim not merely to protect what remains but to put coral back.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: To understand why reefs are struggling, it helps to know that a coral is not a plant or a rock but a colony of small animals called polyps. Inside their tissues live microscopic algae which, through photosynthesis, supply the coral with most of its food and give it its colour. This partnership is sensitive to temperature. When the water stays even one or two degrees above its usual summer maximum for several weeks, the relationship breaks down and the coral expels its algae, turning white. Such bleached corals are not yet dead, and they can recover if conditions return to normal quickly; if the heat persists, however, they starve. Some species cope better than others, but few escape entirely. As oceans have warmed, mass bleaching events that were once rare have become far more frequent, leaving less time for recovery between them.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Heat is not the only problem. As seawater absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, it becomes more acidic, which makes it harder for corals to build their limestone skeletons. Closer to shore, soil and fertiliser washed off farmland cloud the water and encourage the growth of seaweed, while overfishing removes the grazing fish that would normally keep that seaweed in check. Outbreaks of disease, which appear to spread more easily among stressed colonies, add a further threat. A reef weakened by these local pressures is often less able to survive a heatwave.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The most common restoration approach is sometimes called coral gardening. Small pieces are snipped from healthy colonies and hung on underwater frames or ropes, where they grow, protected from predators, until they are large enough to be fixed onto a damaged reef. A refinement of this technique involves cutting certain slow-growing corals into tiny fragments; because the wounded edges heal rapidly, these pieces can spread far faster than an intact colony. Other teams collect the eggs and sperm that corals release during annual spawning events, raise the larvae in tanks and then release them over degraded areas, an approach that can, in principle, cover much larger areas. Most nurseries are run by small organisations that rely heavily on volunteer divers.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: How well does any of this work? A long-term survey led by marine ecologist Talia Gunawardena followed transplanted corals at forty sites for five years. Her team found that the method used mattered less than the place chosen: where the water was clear and herbivorous fish were plentiful, most transplants survived, whereas at sites polluted by run-off, the majority had died by the third year. In Gunawardena's view, restoration cannot succeed unless the local causes of decline are dealt with first. Fisheries researcher Sione Lautaha reached a related conclusion in a village-run project in the Pacific. Survival improved markedly, he reported, once local fishers helped choose sites, because they knew which spots were sheltered from strong currents. He also noted that the villagers who tended the nurseries became more willing to respect fishing restrictions nearby.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: A more ambitious idea is to give corals a better chance against warming itself. Geneticist Beatriz Quintanilla has crossed corals from naturally hot lagoons with those from cooler waters, and in her laboratory trials some offspring withstood temperatures that bleached their cooler-water parents. She warns, though, that these heat-tolerant corals grew noticeably more slowly, and that nobody yet knows whether such traits will remain useful if seas continue to warm. Her next step is to test the crossbred corals on an open reef, where conditions are far less predictable than in a tank.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Cost and scale remain the hardest obstacles. Economist Lars Edvardsen estimated that gardening projects typically spend tens of thousands of dollars to restore a single hectare, while the reefs being damaged each year are measured in thousands of square kilometres. He argues that, in many places, the same money would achieve more if spent on reducing farm run-off or enforcing fishing limits. Few restoration practitioners would disagree that their work cannot replace cuts in greenhouse gas emissions. What restoration can do is buy time: maintaining breeding populations, keeping key sites alive for tourism and coastal protection, and preserving genetic diversity that may prove valuable later. Restoration, in other words, is best seen not as a cure but as one part of a much broader effort, and its success will ultimately depend on decisions taken far from any reef.
paragraphs.label: G

section.text:
Can We Rebuild the Reef?

A. Coral reefs occupy less than one percent of the sea floor, yet they shelter roughly a quarter of all known marine species, protect coastlines from waves and support fisheries and tourism on which hundreds of millions of people depend. Over recent decades, however, many reefs have lost a large share of their living coral, and in some regions the reef that divers see today is a grey, weed-covered skeleton of what existed a generation ago. Against this background, a growing number of projects aim not merely to protect what remains but to put coral back.

B. To understand why reefs are struggling, it helps to know that a coral is not a plant or a rock but a colony of small animals called polyps. Inside their tissues live microscopic algae which, through photosynthesis, supply the coral with most of its food and give it its colour. This partnership is sensitive to temperature. When the water stays even one or two degrees above its usual summer maximum for several weeks, the relationship breaks down and the coral expels its algae, turning white. Such bleached corals are not yet dead, and they can recover if conditions return to normal quickly; if the heat persists, however, they starve. Some species cope better than others, but few escape entirely. As oceans have warmed, mass bleaching events that were once rare have become far more frequent, leaving less time for recovery between them.

C. Heat is not the only problem. As seawater absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, it becomes more acidic, which makes it harder for corals to build their limestone skeletons. Closer to shore, soil and fertiliser washed off farmland cloud the water and encourage the growth of seaweed, while overfishing removes the grazing fish that would normally keep that seaweed in check. Outbreaks of disease, which appear to spread more easily among stressed colonies, add a further threat. A reef weakened by these local pressures is often less able to survive a heatwave.

D. The most common restoration approach is sometimes called coral gardening. Small pieces are snipped from healthy colonies and hung on underwater frames or ropes, where they grow, protected from predators, until they are large enough to be fixed onto a damaged reef. A refinement of this technique involves cutting certain slow-growing corals into tiny fragments; because the wounded edges heal rapidly, these pieces can spread far faster than an intact colony. Other teams collect the eggs and sperm that corals release during annual spawning events, raise the larvae in tanks and then release them over degraded areas, an approach that can, in principle, cover much larger areas. Most nurseries are run by small organisations that rely heavily on volunteer divers.

E. How well does any of this work? A long-term survey led by marine ecologist Talia Gunawardena followed transplanted corals at forty sites for five years. Her team found that the method used mattered less than the place chosen: where the water was clear and herbivorous fish were plentiful, most transplants survived, whereas at sites polluted by run-off, the majority had died by the third year. In Gunawardena's view, restoration cannot succeed unless the local causes of decline are dealt with first. Fisheries researcher Sione Lautaha reached a related conclusion in a village-run project in the Pacific. Survival improved markedly, he reported, once local fishers helped choose sites, because they knew which spots were sheltered from strong currents. He also noted that the villagers who tended the nurseries became more willing to respect fishing restrictions nearby.

F. A more ambitious idea is to give corals a better chance against warming itself. Geneticist Beatriz Quintanilla has crossed corals from naturally hot lagoons with those from cooler waters, and in her laboratory trials some offspring withstood temperatures that bleached their cooler-water parents. She warns, though, that these heat-tolerant corals grew noticeably more slowly, and that nobody yet knows whether such traits will remain useful if seas continue to warm. Her next step is to test the crossbred corals on an open reef, where conditions are far less predictable than in a tank.

G. Cost and scale remain the hardest obstacles. Economist Lars Edvardsen estimated that gardening projects typically spend tens of thousands of dollars to restore a single hectare, while the reefs being damaged each year are measured in thousands of square kilometres. He argues that, in many places, the same money would achieve more if spent on reducing farm run-off or enforcing fishing limits. Few restoration practitioners would disagree that their work cannot replace cuts in greenhouse gas emissions. What restoration can do is buy time: maintaining breeding populations, keeping key sites alive for tourism and coastal protection, and preserving genetic diversity that may prove valuable later. Restoration, in other words, is best seen not as a cure but as one part of a much broader effort, and its success will ultimately depend on decisions taken far from any reef.
